title: Modi's Travel Advisory, a Phantom Tax and the NRI Caught in the Middle
excerpt: The prime minister urged Indians to stay home—then denied plans for a foreign-travel surcharge. For the diaspora, the real story is the policy whiplash between welcoming their dollars and discouraging their trips.
body:
On May 15, Narendra Modi posted a message on X that Indian travel agents had been dreading. The prime minister appealed to citizens to avoid unnecessary foreign travel and cut fuel consumption, citing global energy uncertainty and tensions in West Asia. Within hours, overseas booking inquiries at major agencies fell by 10 to 15 per cent. Shares of Yatra Online and Thomas Cook India slid. And then a rumour, apparently baseless, metastasised: the government was mulling a temporary tax or surcharge on outbound international travel.

Modi himself killed it the same day. "This is totally false," he wrote. "Not an iota of truth in this. There is no question of putting such restrictions on foreign travel. We remain committed to improving 'Ease of Doing Business' and 'Ease of Living' for our people." The denial was unusually emphatic, and it needed to be. India's outbound-travel market is booming—32.7 million departures in 2025, growing at roughly six per cent a year—and the industry that serves it is a major employer.

Yet for the non-resident Indian watching from Houston or Hounslow, the episode was less about a tax that never was than about the policy vertigo that increasingly defines travel between India and everywhere else.

## The Good News Nobody Noticed

Buried in the Budget 2026 fine print was a measure that should have cheered every NRI planning a trip home. The Tax Collected at Source on overseas tour packages was slashed from five per cent to two per cent, effective April 1, 2026. For a family of four booking a ₹5 lakh trip to India through an agent, the upfront tax bite dropped from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000—money eventually adjustable against income tax, but a cash-flow irritant all the same.

The cut was part of a broader liberalisation of the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, designed to make cross-border money movement less punitive. On paper, it was excellent news. In practice, it was drowned out by Modi's "stay home" appeal and the phantom surcharge scare.

## The Forex Squeeze Behind the Rhetoric

The prime minister's appeal did not emerge from nowhere. India's overseas travel spend fell three per cent in the fiscal year ending March 2026, to $15.3 billion from $15.8 billion the year before. The rupee has slid to a record low of ₹95.17 against the dollar; forex reserves have dropped $23 billion in six weeks. For a government watching dollars drain through tourism, remittances and oil imports simultaneously, the temptation to nudge citizens toward domestic holidays is understandable, even if the execution—an off-the-cuff social-media post—was clumsy.

The irony, of course, is that Modi posted his appeal while on a five-nation diplomatic tour himself. Critics were quick to note the dissonance. The broader "Incredible India" domestic-tourism push, a longstanding government priority, gained fresh urgency in the days that followed.

## The Remittance Double Whammy

For NRIs, the travel advisory landed alongside a separate and arguably more consequential threat: a proposed five per cent tax on remittances from the United States, floated by the Trump administration as part of a broader revenue package. India is the world's largest remittance recipient, and the diaspora sends back roughly $125 billion a year. A five per cent levy would effectively impose a toll on the financial lifeline that connects millions of Indian families to their relatives abroad.

Taken together, the two developments—one Indian, one American—sketch a future in which the cost of staying connected to India rises from both ends. The TCS cut is a genuine reprieve, but it is small comfort if Washington taxes the money you send home and Delhi discourages you from visiting.

## What NRIs Should Actually Do

The practical takeaway is less alarming than the headlines suggest. The foreign-travel surcharge does not exist and, per Modi's own words, will not. The TCS cut is real and already in effect. The remittance tax is a proposal, not a law, and faces significant congressional resistance. India's outbound-travel market, powered by a swelling middle class and better air connectivity, is on track to become the world's fifth largest by 2027.

But the episode is a reminder that NRIs occupy a peculiar position in India's economic calculus: courted for their remittances, celebrated at Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, yet implicitly scolded when their travel habits strain the current account. The message, stripped of diplomatic niceties, is simple: send your dollars, but maybe don't come spend them.
